issues.legal_issue: A landlord may appeal under the general civil procedure from the dismissal of an eviction suit when the rent-control law provides no remedy for the landlord against that dismissal.
material_facts: The landlord’s eviction suit under the rent-control law was dismissed by the trial court.
The landlord appealed under the general civil procedure, and the appellate court granted eviction.
A Full Bench of the relevant High Court had held that an appeal was the landlord’s remedy because the rent-control law did not provide a remedy against dismissal of the suit.
issues.conclusion: The appeal from the trial court’s dismissal was maintainable, and the preliminary objection to it was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court agreed with the Full Bench decision in Mohd. Jainul Ansari v. Khalil that Sections 13 and 14 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1982 did not provide the landlord a remedy against dismissal of the eviction suit, so an appeal lay under Section 96 CPC. It distinguished Vinod Kumar Chowdhry v. Smt. Narain Devi Taneja, which concerned a different statutory scheme under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_suit: A landlord brought an eviction suit governed by a rent-control law.
predicates.trial_court_dismissed_landlords_suit: The trial court dismissed the landlord’s eviction suit.
predicates.rent_control_law_provides_no_landlord_re: The rent-control law provides no remedy for a landlord to challenge the trial court’s dismissal of the eviction suit.

issues.definition: When a landlord’s rent-control eviction suit is dismissed and the governing law provides no landlord remedy against that dismissal, the landlord may appeal under the general civil procedure.

issues.legal_issue: A special revision directed against an appellate court’s eviction decree is not maintainable when the statutory revision provision applies only to a trial court’s order for recovery of possession.
material_facts: The appellate court granted the landlord an eviction decree after the trial court had dismissed the suit.
The tenants challenged the appellate decree by filing a revision under the rent-control law.
The statutory revision provision referred to a trial court order for recovery of possession, not an appellate order.
The landlord did not raise the maintainability objection in the High Court, and the Supreme Court treated the revision as a second appeal to meet the ends of justice.
issues.conclusion: The tenants’ revision was not maintainable because it challenged an appellate order, rather than the trial court order covered by the statutory revision provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(8) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1982 provided for revision of a trial court order for recovery of possession, not an appellate order. After an appeal is decided, the further remedy is under Section 100 CPC, not a return to the statutory revision provision. Because the maintainability objection had not been raised in the High Court, the Court treated the proceeding as a second appeal in order to decide it under the restrictions of Section 100 CPC.

predicates.tenant_challenged_appellate_eviction_dec: A tenant challenged an appellate eviction decree by using a special revision procedure.
predicates.special_revision_provision_covers_only_t: The special revision procedure applies only to a trial court’s order for recovery of possession.

issues.definition: When a tenant uses a special revision procedure to challenge an appellate eviction decree, and that procedure covers only trial court possession orders, the revision is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a second appeal cannot interfere with a factual finding by reappreciating evidence when no substantial question of law arises.
material_facts: The High Court’s revision was treated by the Supreme Court as a second appeal.
The High Court reconsidered the evidence concerning the landlord’s bona fide personal requirement and displaced the appellate court’s factual finding.
The appellate court had considered the evidence in detail, and the Supreme Court found that the bona fide requirement issue did not raise a substantial question of law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by reappreciating the evidence and interfering with the appellate court’s factual finding.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 CPC makes the existence of a substantial question of law a sine qua non for exercising second-appellate jurisdiction. The Court relied on Panchugopal Barua v. Umesh Chandra Goswami and Kshitish Chandra Purkait v. Santosh Kumar Purkait. A factual issue of bona fide requirement, decided on an appreciation of evidence, did not raise a substantial question of law here.

predicates.proceeding_is_second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.no_substantial_question_of_law_arises: The dispute does not raise a substantial question of law.
predicates.high_court_reappreciates_evidence_to_dis: The High Court reconsiders the evidence to replace a factual finding made by the appellate court.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, when no substantial question of law arises, a High Court that reappreciates evidence cannot displace the appellate court’s factual finding.

issues.legal_issue: A later eviction suit is not barred by the rule against splitting claims when it rests on a cause of action different from that of the earlier suit.
material_facts: The landlord’s earlier eviction suit relied on non-payment of rent and bona fide personal requirement.
The later eviction suit was brought under the rent-control law on the ground of bona fide personal requirement.
The Court found that the cause of action for the later suit was entirely different from the cause of action for the earlier suit.
issues.conclusion: The later eviction suit was not barred by Order 2 Rule 2 CPC.
issues.legal_principle: Order 2 Rule 2 CPC does not bar a later suit where its cause of action is different from the cause of action for the earlier suit. The Court concluded that the cause of action for the later eviction suit was entirely different from that of the earlier suit.

predicates.later_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a later suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.later_suit_has_different_cause_of_action: The cause of action for the later eviction suit differs from the cause of action for the earlier suit.

issues.definition: A later eviction suit based on a cause of action different from the earlier suit is not barred by the claim-splitting rule.
